marrow__ANAT_CH53_Q001.takeaway: The marked ligament is lacunar (Gimbernat) ligament, which forms the medial wall of the femoral canal and attaches to the pecten pubis.
marrow__ANAT_CH53_Q001.displayText:
The marked ligament is lacunar (Gimbernat) ligament, which forms the medial wall of the femoral canal and attaches to the pecten pubis.

The structure marked is the lacunar ligament.

Lacunar (Gimbernat's) ligament is a thick triangular band of tissue formed from fibres of the medial end of the inguinal ligament and fascia lata. It forms the medial wall of the femoral canal, and the apex of the triangle is attached to the pubic tubercle.

The inguinal (Poupart's) ligament is the thickened external oblique aponeurosis stretched between the ASIS and pubic tubercle. The pectineal (Astley-Cooper's) ligament is a strong fibrous band extending laterally along the pectineal line from the pectineal attachment of the lacunar ligament. The conjoint tendon is formed by the common aponeurosis of internal oblique and transversus abdominis and inserts into the pubic crest/pectineal line.
emphasis: The marked ligament is lacunar (Gimbernat) ligament, which forms the medial wall of the femoral canal and attaches to the pecten pubis

rationales.a: Poupart's (inguinal) ligament spans the ASIS to pubic tubercle; the source marker identifies the medial triangular lacunar extension.
rationales.c: Cooper's pectineal ligament runs along the pecten pubis, not the triangular medial inguinal-fold structure shown.
rationales.d: The conjoint tendon is the fused internal oblique/transversus aponeurosis, not the marked ligament.

marrow__ANAT_CH53_Q002.takeaway: The iliopubic tract is a thickened transversalis fascia posterior to the inguinal ligament, whose lateral fibers blend with fascia iliaca.
marrow__ANAT_CH53_Q002.displayText:
The iliopubic tract is a thickened transversalis fascia posterior to the inguinal ligament, whose lateral fibers blend with fascia iliaca.

The fibres of the iliopubic tract fan out with fascia iliaca laterally.

The iliopubic tract is a thickening of the transversalis fascia lying immediately posterior to the inguinal (Poupart's) ligament. It extends from the ASIS superolaterally and arches across the front of the femoral sheath.

Medially, its fibres insert broadly into the pubic tubercle and pectineal line behind the conjoint tendon. Laterally, its fibres fan out within the transversalis fascia and fascia iliaca without bony attachment to the iliac spines.

Clinical note: it is an important landmark in laparoscopic hernia surgery.
emphasis: The iliopubic tract is a thickened transversalis fascia posterior to the inguinal ligament, whose lateral fibers blend with fascia iliaca

rationales.a: The tract is a transversalis fascia thickening, not a lumbar-fascia thickening.
rationales.b: It lies immediately posterior to Poupart's ligament rather than anterior to it.
rationales.c: Medially it attaches behind the conjoint tendon, not in front of it.

marrow__ANAT_CH53_Q003.takeaway: The bony pelvis consists of the two hip bones, sacrum and coccyx; L5 is superior to the pelvic ring.
marrow__ANAT_CH53_Q003.displayText:
The bony pelvis consists of the two hip bones, sacrum and coccyx; L5 is superior to the pelvic ring.

The L5 lumbar vertebra does not form the bony pelvis.

The bony pelvis consists of two hip bones, the sacrum, and the coccyx. Their articulations form two sacroiliac joints, the sacrococcygeal symphysis, and the pubic symphysis.
emphasis: The bony pelvis consists of the two hip bones, sacrum and coccyx; L5 is superior to the pelvic ring

rationales.a: The pubis is one component of each hip bone and contributes to the anterior pelvis.
rationales.b: The ilium is part of the hip bone and forms the superior/lateral pelvis.
rationales.d: The coccyx articulates with the sacrum and contributes to the posterior bony pelvis.

marrow__ANAT_CH53_Q004.takeaway: The pelvic inlet is bounded by the sacral promontory, arcuate/pectineal lines and pubic symphysis; ischial tuberosities bound the outlet.
marrow__ANAT_CH53_Q004.displayText:
The pelvic inlet is bounded by the sacral promontory, arcuate/pectineal lines and pubic symphysis; ischial tuberosities bound the outlet.

The structure involved in cephalopelvic disproportion at the level of the inlet is the pelvic inlet. The ischial tuberosity does not form a boundary of the pelvic inlet.

Boundaries of the pelvic inlet: posteriorly the sacral promontory; laterally the arcuate line on the medial surface of the ilium and the pectineal line on the superior pubic ramus; anteriorly the pubic symphysis.

Boundaries of the pelvic outlet: posteriorly the tip of the coccyx; laterally the ischial tuberosities and inferior margin of the sacrotuberous ligament; anteriorly the pubic arch.

Clinical significance: cephalopelvic disproportion can occur when inlet or outlet diameters are shortened enough to prevent engagement of the fetal head.
emphasis: The pelvic inlet is bounded by the sacral promontory, arcuate/pectineal lines and pubic symphysis; ischial tuberosities bound the outlet

rationales.a: The sacral promontory forms the posterior boundary of the pelvic inlet.
rationales.c: The pecten pubis is part of the pelvic brim and contributes to the inlet boundary.
rationales.d: The pubic symphysis forms the anterior boundary of the pelvic inlet.

marrow__ANAT_CH53_Q005.takeaway: The marked muscle is piriformis, a sacral muscle closely related to the sciatic nerve as it exits the pelvis.
marrow__ANAT_CH53_Q005.displayText:
The marked muscle is piriformis, a sacral muscle closely related to the sciatic nerve as it exits the pelvis.

The marked muscle is the piriformis muscle.

Origin: anterior surface of sacrum, posterior inferior iliac spine, capsule of sacroiliac joint, and sacrotuberous ligament. Insertion: greater trochanter of femur. Action: lateral rotation of the thigh in extension and abduction of the thigh in the flexed position.

Piriformis forms the posterolateral wall of the pelvic cavity. The sciatic nerve is closely related and may pass through its fibres or below the muscle.

Clinical significance: piriformis syndrome is compression of the sciatic nerve by the piriformis, often associated with pain along the sciatic distribution (sciatica).
emphasis: The marked muscle is piriformis, a sacral muscle closely related to the sciatic nerve as it exits the pelvis

rationales.b: Gemellus superior is a short lateral rotator below piriformis, not the larger marked muscle forming part of the posterior pelvic wall.
rationales.c: Gluteus minimus lies on the lateral ilium and inserts on the greater trochanter; it is not the marked deep pelvic muscle.
rationales.d: Quadratus femoris is an inferior short lateral rotator extending from ischial tuberosity to femur, distinct from piriformis.

marrow__ANAT_CH53_Q006.takeaway: Obturator internus and its fascia form the anterolateral wall of the true pelvis.
marrow__ANAT_CH53_Q006.displayText:
Obturator internus and its fascia form the anterolateral wall of the true pelvis.

Obturator internus with its fascia forms the anterolateral wall of the true pelvis.

Muscles forming the walls of the true pelvis: anterolateral wall — obturator internus and fascia over its upper and inner surface; posterolateral wall — piriformis; floor — levator ani and coccygeus.
emphasis: Obturator internus and its fascia form the anterolateral wall of the true pelvis

rationales.a: Obturator externus lies outside the pelvic cavity and does not line the true-pelvis wall.
rationales.b: Piriformis forms the posterolateral, not anterolateral, wall of the true pelvis.
rationales.d: Levator ani forms the pelvic floor rather than the anterolateral wall.

marrow__ANAT_CH53_Q007.takeaway: The levator ani comprises puborectalis, pubococcygeus and iliococcygeus; ischiococcygeus is a separate coccygeus muscle.
marrow__ANAT_CH53_Q007.displayText:
The levator ani comprises puborectalis, pubococcygeus and iliococcygeus; ischiococcygeus is a separate coccygeus muscle.

The scenario and image depict uterine prolapse, which can occur due to weakness of the levator ani. Ischiococcygeus is not part of the levator ani and therefore is not one of the muscles whose weakness produces this support failure.

Levator ani forms a large portion of the pelvic floor and is composed of pubococcygeus, puborectalis, and iliococcygeus.
emphasis: The levator ani comprises puborectalis, pubococcygeus and iliococcygeus; ischiococcygeus is a separate coccygeus muscle

rationales.a: Puborectalis is part of levator ani and its sling helps support pelvic viscera and maintain the anorectal angle.
rationales.b: Pubococcygeus is a component of levator ani and contributes to pelvic-organ support.
rationales.d: Iliococcygeus is the posterior portion of levator ani and weakness can impair pelvic-floor support.

marrow__ANAT_CH53_Q008.takeaway: Levator ani arises partly from the tendinous arch in obturator fascia, not from piriformis fascia.
marrow__ANAT_CH53_Q008.displayText:
Levator ani arises partly from the tendinous arch in obturator fascia, not from piriformis fascia.

The levator ani arises from a condensation of obturator fascia forming the tendinous arch of levator ani, not from piriformis fascia.

The vaginal, urethral, and rectal hiatuses are occluded by contraction of levator ani and relaxation is needed for defecation and urination. Pubococcygeus and puborectalis help maintain rectal tone and create the anorectal angle.
emphasis: Levator ani arises partly from the tendinous arch in obturator fascia, not from piriformis fascia

rationales.a: Levator ani contraction narrows the pelvic hiatuses, including the vaginal canal, so this is not the false statement.
rationales.b: Puborectalis forms the anorectal sling; pubococcygeus contributes to pelvic-floor support and rectal continence.
rationales.c: Pelvic-floor tone supports the anorectal angle and contributes to rectal continence.

marrow__ANAT_CH53_Q009.takeaway: The internal pudendal artery arises from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery and supplies perineal structures.
marrow__ANAT_CH53_Q009.displayText:
The internal pudendal artery arises from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery and supplies perineal structures.

The anterior division of the internal iliac artery gives rise to the internal pudendal artery.

The internal iliac artery divides at the superior border of the greater sciatic foramen into anterior and posterior trunks.

Anterior-trunk branches listed in the source include obturator, superior vesical, inferior vesical, inferior gluteal, middle rectal, vaginal (female), uterine (female), and internal pudendal arteries. Posterior-trunk branches include iliolumbar, lateral sacral, and superior gluteal arteries.
emphasis: The internal pudendal artery arises from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery and supplies perineal structures

rationales.b: The posterior division gives iliolumbar, lateral sacral and superior gluteal branches; internal pudendal arises anteriorly.
rationales.c: The external iliac continues as the femoral artery and does not give rise to internal pudendal.
rationales.d: The iliolumbar artery is a posterior-division branch, not the parent vessel of internal pudendal.

marrow__ANAT_CH53_Q010.takeaway: The inferior epigastric artery forms the lateral boundary of Hesselbach's triangle and branches from the external iliac artery.
marrow__ANAT_CH53_Q010.displayText:
The inferior epigastric artery forms the lateral boundary of Hesselbach's triangle and branches from the external iliac artery.

The lateral boundary of Hesselbach's triangle is formed by the inferior epigastric artery, which originates from the external iliac artery.

Branches of the external iliac artery include the deep circumflex iliac and inferior epigastric arteries, small branches to psoas major and nearby lymph nodes, and continuation as the femoral artery.

Clinical significance: the inferior epigastric artery contributes to the corona mortis; injury in this region can cause severe hemorrhage.
emphasis: The inferior epigastric artery forms the lateral boundary of Hesselbach's triangle and branches from the external iliac artery

rationales.a: The internal iliac anterior trunk supplies pelvic structures; it is not the origin of the inferior epigastric artery.
rationales.b: The internal iliac posterior trunk gives iliolumbar, lateral sacral and superior gluteal branches.
rationales.d: The femoral artery is the continuation of external iliac below the inguinal ligament, not the origin of inferior epigastric.

marrow__ANAT_CH53_Q011.takeaway: The median sacral vein commonly drains to a common iliac vein; superior and inferior gluteal veins are internal iliac tributaries.
marrow__ANAT_CH53_Q011.displayText:
The median sacral vein commonly drains to a common iliac vein; superior and inferior gluteal veins are internal iliac tributaries.

The median sacral vein is a tributary of the common iliac vein.

Tributaries of the common iliac vein include median sacral, iliolumbar, and occasionally lateral sacral veins. Internal iliac tributaries include superior and inferior gluteal, internal pudendal, obturator, lateral sacral, middle rectal, vesical, and uterine/vaginal veins. External iliac tributaries include inferior epigastric, deep circumflex iliac, and pubic veins.

Clinical note: agenesis of the external iliac vein has been reported in association with Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome.
emphasis: The median sacral vein commonly drains to a common iliac vein; superior and inferior gluteal veins are internal iliac tributaries

rationales.a: The middle rectal vein usually drains to the internal iliac system rather than directly to the common iliac vein.
rationales.b: The superior gluteal vein is an internal iliac tributary.
rationales.c: The inferior gluteal vein drains to the internal iliac vein, not the common iliac directly.

marrow__ANAT_CH53_Q012.takeaway: The pudendal nerve hooks around the ischial spine between the greater and lesser sciatic foramina, a landmark for nerve block.
marrow__ANAT_CH53_Q012.displayText:
The pudendal nerve hooks around the ischial spine between the greater and lesser sciatic foramina, a landmark for nerve block.

The highlighted red structure is the ischial spine and the pudendal nerve is related to it.

The pudendal nerve arises from S2-S4, exits the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen, and enters the perineum by passing around the ischial spine. The ischial spine is used as a landmark for pudendal nerve block.
emphasis: The pudendal nerve hooks around the ischial spine between the greater and lesser sciatic foramina, a landmark for nerve block

rationales.b: The sciatic nerve exits below piriformis through the greater sciatic foramen and does not hook around the ischial spine into the perineum.
rationales.c: The obturator nerve passes through the obturator canal to the medial thigh, not around the ischial spine.
rationales.d: The femoral nerve passes deep to the inguinal ligament into the anterior thigh rather than around the ischial spine.

marrow__ANAT_CH53_Q013.takeaway: The perineum's posterior boundary is the coccyx; sacrotuberous ligaments form posterolateral boundaries, while sacrospinous ligaments do not define the surface diamond.
marrow__ANAT_CH53_Q013.displayText:
The perineum's posterior boundary is the coccyx; sacrotuberous ligaments form posterolateral boundaries, while sacrospinous ligaments do not define the surface diamond.

The sacrospinous ligament does not form an anatomical boundary of the perineum.

The perineum is a diamond-shaped region overlying the pelvic outlet. Its boundaries are: anteriorly the pubic symphysis and arcuate ligament; posteriorly the coccyx; anterolaterally the ischiopubic rami and ischial tuberosities; posterolaterally the sacrotuberous ligaments.
emphasis: The perineum's posterior boundary is the coccyx; sacrotuberous ligaments form posterolateral boundaries, while sacrospinous ligaments do not define the surface diamond

rationales.a: The arcuate pubic ligament contributes to the anterior boundary at the pubic arch.
rationales.b: The sacrotuberous ligaments form posterolateral boundaries of the perineal diamond.
rationales.d: The coccyx marks the posterior boundary of the perineum.

marrow__ANAT_CH53_Q014.takeaway: A line between the ischial tuberosities separates the anterior urogenital triangle from the posterior anal triangle.
marrow__ANAT_CH53_Q014.displayText:
A line between the ischial tuberosities separates the anterior urogenital triangle from the posterior anal triangle.

An imaginary line joining the two ischial tuberosities divides the perineum into an anterior urogenital triangle and a posterior anal/anogenital triangle.

The urogenital triangle faces downwards and forwards. In males it contains the scrotum and root of the penis; in females, the mons pubis and labia with the vestibule. The anal triangle faces downwards and backwards and contains the anal canal with its sphincters and the ischioanal fossae.
emphasis: A line between the ischial tuberosities separates the anterior urogenital triangle from the posterior anal triangle

rationales.a: The ischial spines are landmarks for the pelvic outlet and pudendal nerve but do not divide the perineal triangles.
rationales.b: The symphysis-to-promontory line lies along the pelvic axis, not across the perineum between its triangles.
rationales.d: The symphysis-to-coccyx median line follows the anteroposterior axis rather than dividing anterior and posterior triangles.
